title: A continuous integral dominating pivot splits off locally
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime and let $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ be finite with valuation ring $A=\mathcal O_E$ and valuation topology [def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension]. Let $\pi$ generate the maximal ideal of $A$. Let $T$ be a topological space, let $m,n\geq1$, and let $G:T\to\operatorname{Mat}_{n\times m}(A)$ have continuous entries. Fix $e\geq0$ and $t_0\in T$. Assume every entry of $G(t)$ lies in $\pi^eA$ for every $t\in T$, and $G_{11}(t_0)\in\pi^eA^\times$. Then there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $t_0$, entrywise continuous maps $L:U\to\operatorname{GL}_n(A)$ and $R:U\to\operatorname{GL}_m(A)$ with entrywise continuous inverses, and a matrix $H:U\to\operatorname{Mat}_{(n-1)\times(m-1)}(A)$ with continuous entries such that
$$L(t)G(t)R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\pi^e&0\\0&H(t)\end{pmatrix}\qquad(t\in U).$$
Here $\operatorname{GL}_q(A)$ denotes the invertible square matrices; the smaller matrix may have zero rows or columns. No local constancy of a cokernel is assumed.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: comparison of valuations makes division integral. Agent local nowhere-zero pivot variant, extracted from step 2 of lem-sfb-continuous-integral-matrix-local-smith; explicit construction in the repair report, not a theorem stated in HRS.

proof.text: Set $q_{ij}(t)$ to be the quotient of $G_{ij}(t)$ by $\pi^e$. The divisibility hypothesis and [lem-sfb-continuous-uniformizer-division] give entrywise continuous maps $q:T\to\operatorname{Mat}_{n\times m}(A)$ with $G=\pi^e q$. At $t_0$, $q_{11}(t_0)$ is a unit; after shrinking to an open neighbourhood $U$ of $t_0$, the same lemma gives that $a(t)=q_{11}(t)$ is unit-valued and $a^{-1}$ is continuous on $U$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: comparison of valuations makes division integral.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-unit-pivot-schur-formula] to $q|_U$ and the pivot $a$. Write the combined left factor supplied there as $L_{\mathrm{pivot}}(t)=L_0(t)L_1(t)$. Its explicit diagonal and transvection matrices are continuous and invertible with continuous inverses, and they give $L_{\mathrm{pivot}}(t)q(t)R_0(t)=\operatorname{diag}(1,H_0(t))$ for a continuous residual block $H_0(t)$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: elementary row and column elimination after integral division.

proof.text: Multiply the identity in the previous step by the scalar $\pi^e$. Define $L=L_{\mathrm{pivot}}$, $R=R_0$, and $H=\pi^eH_0$ entrywise. Then $L(t)G(t)R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\pi^e&0\\0&H(t)\end{pmatrix}$, and continuity of $H$ follows from continuity of $H_0$ and scalar multiplication in $A$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: normalization of the pivot and block identity.

proof.text: When $n=1$ or $m=1$, the reduced block has zero rows or columns and the same formulas are interpreted as empty matrices; the identities and continuity assertions remain valid. Thus the constructed $U,L,R,H$ satisfy every clause of the statement.
